meta.subtitle: Q2 FY27 ARR $5.84B (+25%), net new ARR $333M; a wide-moat franchise fully valued above the Street's target -- HOLD.

analystCommentary: We rate CrowdStrike HOLD with a $220-$305 target range. The second quarter of fiscal 2027, ended July 31, 2026, was strong on every operating metric: total revenue rose 26% to $1.47 billion, subscription revenue rose 27% to $1.40 billion, annual recurring revenue grew 25% year-over-year to $5.84 billion, and the company added $333 million of net new ARR, up 51%. Falcon Flex ending ARR exceeded $2.29 billion, up 101%. Cash generation was strong, with operating cash flow of $530.3 million and free cash flow of $377.4 million, both quarterly highs the company flagged. The problem is price, not the business. At $261.28 the stock trades at 49.6x sales and about 208x next-twelve-month earnings, and it sits above the Street's consensus target of $235.67 (median $245.00, range $132.00-$300.00). GAAP earnings are near breakeven -- second-quarter GAAP diluted EPS was $0.01 and non-GAAP $0.31 -- so we anchor on ARR, net new ARR and free cash flow rather than a GAAP multiple. Our probability-weighted fair value is near $255, about 2% below the current price, against a bear-case downside near 29%; that risk/reward is unattractive even for a wide-moat franchise, which holds the rating at HOLD. The Street is more constructive, at 40 buy, 12 hold and 1 sell.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: CrowdStrike Holdings, Inc. (Nasdaq: CRWD), incorporated in 2011 and headquartered in Austin, Texas, provides cloud-delivered cybersecurity through its AI-native Falcon platform, sold on a SaaS subscription model with a single lightweight sensor. The platform protects endpoints, cloud workloads, identity and data, and spans managed security, threat intelligence, next-generation SIEM, identity protection and AI-workload security. The company sells through a partner-first, land-and-expand model: customers start with any number of cloud modules and add capabilities over time, and Falcon Flex, its enterprise licensing model, lets customers commit to a broad platform investment upfront and draw it down across products. Module adoption is deepening -- as of July 31, 2026, 51% of subscription customers had adopted six or more modules, 35% seven or more, and 26% eight or more. Revenue is recognized ratably over one-to-three-year subscription terms, so reported revenue lags bookings and the ARR base is the leading indicator. The company reports as a single reportable segment and breaks out no product or geographic revenue split. Strategic alliances span Cognizant, Snowflake, Fortanix, Cerebras Systems, Amazon Web Services and Schwarz Digits; the company agreed to acquire the technology assets of XM Cyber. Fiscal 2027 revenue is guided to $5,991.1-$6,011.1 million.

thesis.body: CrowdStrike is a high-quality compounder whose price already discounts years of that compounding. The bull case is the operating record: ARR of $5.84 billion growing 25%, net new ARR of $333 million, Falcon Flex ARR above $2.29 billion growing 101%, a 74.7% gross margin, and fiscal 2026 free cash flow of $1.3 billion at a 27.2% margin -- a rare pairing of scale, growth and cash generation. The counter-case is valuation and the durability of the multiple. At 49.6x sales and about 208x forward earnings, with the shares above the consensus target of $235.67, the market already prices sustained high-20s ARR growth and margin expansion. A growth slowdown, a renewed drag from the July 19, 2024 Incident, or a broad de-rating of high-multiple software would each compress the multiple faster than fundamentals improve. GAAP profitability remains marginal, so the equity is valued on ARR and free cash flow, both of which must keep compounding to justify the price. We see a wide moat fully valued, not a bargain.

catalysts: Raised outlook: management increased its fiscal 2027 net new ARR growth guidance by 630 basis points to 34% at the midpoint, and guides full-year revenue to $5,991.1-$6,011.1 million and non-GAAP EPS to $1.25-$1.26.
Falcon Flex adoption: ending Falcon Flex ARR extended its rapid year-over-year climb, evidence the enterprise licensing model is pulling broader, larger platform commitments.
Module expansion: a growing share of subscription customers run six or more modules, the mechanism behind expansion within the existing base.
Cash generation: second-quarter free cash flow reached $377.4 million, funding investment and future buyback capacity without external capital.
AI-security demand: new offerings such as Continuous Identity for AI Agents and Falcon AIDR, plus alliances with AWS, Cerebras and Schwarz Digits, extend the platform into securing AI workloads.
risks: Valuation: the stock trades at a rich multiple of sales and of forward earnings and sits above the consensus target, so the price leaves little margin of safety if growth or the multiple slips.

July 19 Incident: the 2024 Falcon sensor outage has elongated sales cycles and raised contraction, and still carries lawsuits and customer-commitment discounting; management expects continued effects.
GAAP profitability: GAAP results are near breakeven (second-quarter diluted EPS $0.01; fiscal 2026 diluted EPS -$0.65), so the equity depends on ARR and free cash flow rather than reported earnings.
Growth deceleration: annual revenue growth has slowed from 54.4% in fiscal 2023 to 21.7% in fiscal 2026, and net retention can fall if customers renew with shorter terms or fewer modules.
Competition: the company faces intense competition, and certain rivals approached its customers and partners after the July 19 Incident.

financials.incomeCommentary: In the second quarter of fiscal 2027 (ended July 31, 2026), total revenue rose 26% to $1.47 billion and subscription revenue rose 27% to $1.40 billion, from $1.17 billion a year earlier. GAAP subscription gross margin was 78%, up from 77%, and non-GAAP subscription gross margin was 81%. The GAAP loss from operations narrowed to $33.2 million from $105.5 million, while non-GAAP income from operations rose to $371.6 million from $255.0 million; the gap is largely stock-based compensation, acquisition and July 19 Incident costs. GAAP net income attributable to CrowdStrike was $5.3 million, or $0.01 per diluted share, against a $70.2 million loss a year earlier; non-GAAP net income was $322.9 million, or $0.31 per diluted share, up from $0.23. On a full-year basis the picture is growth decelerating as the base scales: revenue rose from $1.5 billion in fiscal 2022 to $4.8 billion in fiscal 2026, with year-over-year growth easing from 54.4% to 21.7%. Fiscal 2026 carried a 74.7% gross margin, a -6.1% GAAP operating margin and a diluted loss of $0.65 per share; fiscal 2024 was the one profitable year at $0.30. The vendor's snapshot labels the July quarter as 'Q3 2026'; we use the company's own label, the second quarter of fiscal 2027, throughout. Prior-year interim figures were revised for an immaterial error found in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026.
financials.balanceCommentary: CrowdStrike's balance sheet is a fortress. At fiscal 2026 year-end it held $5.2 billion of cash and short-term investments against $0.7 billion of total debt, a net cash position of $4.5 billion, and cash and cash equivalents grew to $5.01 billion by July 31, 2026. Total equity was of similar size and the current ratio was 1.77 at year-end, 1.57 on a trailing-twelve-month basis. Total debt has held near that level across the five-year record while cash compounded from $2.0 billion in fiscal 2022, so leverage is not a concern; the -5.0x interest-coverage figure reflects the near-breakeven operating line, not a solvency issue, because the company carries far more cash than debt. The equity base has more than quadrupled from $1.0 billion in fiscal 2022, built from retained cash flow rather than issuance-heavy funding. The net-cash position gives management room to invest, to acquire -- as with the agreed purchase of XM Cyber's technology assets -- and to repurchase stock without external capital.
financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation is the cleanest measure of CrowdStrike's quality. In the second quarter of fiscal 2027 operating cash flow was $530.3 million, up from $332.8 million, and free cash flow was $377.4 million, up from $283.6 million. On a full-year basis fiscal 2026 operating cash flow was $1.6 billion and free cash flow $1.3 billion, a 27.2% free-cash-flow margin, on capital expenditure of about $302 million. Free cash flow has compounded every year, from $0.5 billion in fiscal 2022, even as GAAP earnings stayed near breakeven: the ratable subscription model collects cash upfront and recognizes revenue over the contract term, so operating cash flow runs well ahead of reported income. The company pays no dividend and reported no share repurchases across the five-year record, so free cash flow has accumulated on the balance sheet as net cash. The gap between strong free cash flow and marginal GAAP earnings is driven largely by stock-based compensation, which is the central tension for a shareholder: the cash is real, but so is the dilution that the non-GAAP add-backs set aside.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: At $261.28 CrowdStrike trades at 49.6x trailing sales and about 208x next-twelve-month earnings; the trailing P/E of -6,531.9x is meaningless because GAAP earnings are near zero, and there is no EV/EBITDA line because EBITDA is not reported. For a subscription franchise the relevant anchors are ARR and free cash flow, and against sales that multiple is among the richest in software. Growth is strong -- consensus sees revenue rising from $4.8 billion in fiscal 2026 to about $6.0 billion in fiscal 2027 and $7.4 billion in fiscal 2028, with non-GAAP EPS of $1.26 and $1.61 -- but at about 162.7x estimated fiscal 2028 earnings the price already extrapolates that trajectory. Peer multiples are pending a peer data source, so we anchor to the company's own history and to the Street: the consensus target of $235.67 sits 9.8% below the current price, the median is $245.00, and the range runs $132.00-$300.00. That the average analyst target implies downside, even as most analysts rate the stock a buy, captures the tension -- a strong business at a price that already reflects it.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: ARR growth holds in the mid-20s as Falcon Flex and module adoption compound, free cash flow keeps expanding, and the high-multiple software group holds its rating; the stock re-rates toward the top of the Street's $300.00 range and beyond as fiscal 2028 estimates rise.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Revenue growth moderates toward the low-20s in line with guidance, the rich sales multiple compresses modestly, and free-cash-flow growth roughly offsets the de-rating; the stock hovers near the current level and the consensus median target of $245.00.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: Net new ARR growth slows, the July 19 Incident's contraction effects linger, or high-multiple software de-rates broadly; the 49.6x sales multiple compresses sharply and the stock falls toward $185, still well above its 52-week low of $85.68.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight the Base at 45%, the Bull at 30% and the Bear at 25%. That yields a probability-weighted fair value near $255, about 2% below the current $261.28, with a bear-case downside near 29% to a Bear price of $185. The reward/risk is unattractive: the expected value sits slightly below today's price while the bear case is a large drawdown, so on the derived rule the signal is HOLD, and we rate it HOLD. The asymmetry follows from valuation, not from the business -- at 49.6x sales the stock needs high-20s ARR growth and margin expansion to persist merely to hold its multiple, and the consensus target already implies 9.8% downside. That Bear outcome is a real scenario, a de-rating of high-multiple software rather than a fundamental collapse, and it still sits far above the 52-week low of $85.68. Our $220-$305 target range brackets the Base implied price and straddles the current price, reflecting a franchise we would own at a lower entry but not chase here.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: CrowdStrike reports as a single reportable segment and discloses no product or geographic revenue split, so the consolidated total is the reportable line: fiscal 2026 revenue of $4.8 billion, essentially all subscription. Within that total, annual recurring revenue reached $5.84 billion at July 31, 2026, up 25%, with net new ARR of $333 million in the quarter. Subscription gross margin runs high -- 78% GAAP and 81% non-GAAP in the second quarter -- reflecting the scale economics of a single cloud platform delivered through one lightweight sensor. Professional services are a small, deliberately loss-leading complement used to cross-sell Falcon subscriptions. Because the company sells one platform with many modules rather than distinct product lines, the moat is best read at the platform level: more modules per customer, more data, and a stronger network effect.

moatFactors.name: Platform and single-sensor architecture
moatFactors.body: Falcon is delivered as one cloud-native platform through a single lightweight sensor, so customers add modules without deploying new agents. Module adoption is deepening -- 51% of subscription customers run six or more modules, 35% seven or more, and 26% eight or more as of July 31, 2026 -- which raises switching costs and spreads the platform's fixed cost across more revenue per customer.

moatFactors.name: Network effect from data scale
moatFactors.body: The Security Cloud correlates trillions of security events each week; the company states that more data fed into Falcon makes its detection more effective, a self-reinforcing advantage that a subscale rival struggles to replicate. A $5.84 billion ARR base and continued net new ARR growth widen that data and installed-base lead.

moatFactors.name: Land-and-expand and Falcon Flex
moatFactors.body: The land-and-expand model and the Falcon Flex licensing framework let customers commit broadly upfront and draw down across products; Falcon Flex ending ARR surpassed $2.29 billion, up 101% year-over-year, evidence that customers are consolidating security spend onto the platform.

moatFactors.name: Switching costs
moatFactors.body: Once a customer standardizes on Falcon across endpoints, cloud and identity, replacing it means re-instrumenting security operations. High dollar-based gross retention persisted even through the July 19 Incident, though the incident showed the retention is not unconditional.

businessMoat.durability: The moat is wide but not unconditional. The platform, the data-scale network effect and multi-module adoption make CrowdStrike costly to displace, and ARR and free cash flow have compounded through a threat environment that keeps security demand growing. The clearest threat to durability is self-inflicted: the July 19, 2024 Incident showed that a single faulty update can elongate sales cycles, invite competitor poaching and force customer-commitment discounting that raises contraction, even when gross retention holds. Competition is intense, and pricing is disciplined by rivals rather than by CrowdStrike alone. The second threat is expectations, not economics: at 49.6x sales the equity is valued for sustained high-20s ARR growth and margin expansion, so even a healthy deceleration -- annual revenue growth has already slowed markedly since fiscal 2023 -- can compress the multiple. We rate the moat wide and the business durable, but the equity's risk sits in the valuation rather than the franchise.

points: Annual recurring revenue reached $5.84 billion at July 31, 2026, up 25%, with $333 million of net new ARR added in the quarter, up 51%, and $588.6 million over the six months.
Falcon Flex ending ARR surpassed $2.29 billion, up 101% year-over-year, as the enterprise licensing model pulls larger, broader platform commitments.
Management raised the fiscal 2027 net new ARR growth outlook by 630 basis points to 34% at the midpoint and guides full-year revenue to $5,991.1-$6,011.1 million.
Module adoption deepened to 51% of subscription customers on six or more modules, the mechanism behind expansion within the existing base.

Consensus sees revenue reaching about $6.0 billion in fiscal 2027 and $7.4 billion in fiscal 2028, with non-GAAP EPS of $1.26 and $1.61, though annual growth continues to decelerate as the base scales.
AI security is an emerging vector: offerings such as Continuous Identity for AI Agents and Falcon AIDR, and alliances with AWS, Cerebras and Schwarz Digits, target securing enterprise AI workloads.

management.leadership: George Kurtz, the company's founder, is Chief Executive Officer, and Burt W. Podbere is Chief Financial Officer. On the second-quarter results Kurtz highlighted the Falcon Flex results and net new ARR, and Podbere pointed to strong quarterly cash flow from operations and free cash flow and to the raised full-year net new ARR outlook. The team's execution shows in the ARR, net new ARR and free-cash-flow figures set out above, but the same team presided over the July 19, 2024 Incident and the customer-commitment discounting that followed, and revised prior-year interim financials for an immaterial error found in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026. Founder leadership aligns management with the long-term platform strategy; the incident and the revision are reminders that execution risk is real.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation is investment-led and internally funded. The company pays no dividend and reported no share repurchases across the five-year record, so the roughly $1.3 billion of fiscal 2026 free cash flow has accumulated as net cash, which reached $4.5 billion at year-end. Reinvestment runs through research and development and sales and marketing to sustain the land-and-expand model, and through acquisitions that extend the platform -- most recently the agreed purchase of XM Cyber's technology assets from Schwarz Digits. Capital expenditure is modest at about $302 million in fiscal 2026. The net-cash balance sheet and strong free cash flow give management ample capacity to keep investing, to acquire and eventually to return capital, though stock-based compensation -- the main reconciling item between GAAP and non-GAAP results -- is a form of dilution that free-cash-flow figures do not capture. We would want to see buybacks begin to offset that dilution as the company matures.
management.governance: Governance rests on the 2026 proxy statement (DEF 14A, filed May 5, 2026). As of April 3, 2026, 254,580,533 shares of Class A common stock were outstanding and no Class B shares remained outstanding, so the historical dual-class structure no longer concentrates votes in a separate super-voting class. The founder, George Kurtz, serves as Chief Executive Officer and a director, aligning management with shareholders, and the proxy names independent directors and director nominees. The captured excerpt covers the beneficial-ownership table rather than the full board and compensation discussion, so we do not infer board-independence counts or committee structure beyond what it supports; related-party detail beyond ordinary beneficial ownership is not in the excerpt.
management.insiderOwnership: Beneficial ownership is disclosed as of April 3, 2026, against 254,580,533 Class A shares outstanding. Founder and Chief Executive Officer George Kurtz beneficially owned 2,384,082 shares, less than 1%, including shares held through trusts and options exercisable within 60 days. All executive officers and directors as a group (11 persons) owned 4,262,065 shares, or 1.67%. Among outside holders, The Vanguard Group reported 18,449,066 shares, or 7.27%, and BlackRock, Inc. reported 16,954,069 shares, or 6.70%. Insider ownership is modest in percentage terms, so alignment rests on the founder's role and equity incentives rather than a controlling stake; the reported blocks above five percent sit with index managers, which typically support management. The low insider percentage also means stock-based compensation, not founder control, is the main channel through which the broad employee base participates in the equity.

idiosyncratic: July 19, 2024 Incident: the faulty Falcon sensor update caused Windows system crashes and has led to lawsuits, elongated sales cycles, delayed purchasing decisions and customer-commitment packages featuring discounts, extra modules and extended terms. Management expects the incident to keep raising costs and to pressure key metrics in future periods, and because contracts run over a year, churn and contraction can surface with a lag.

Valuation and expectations: at 49.6x sales and about 208x forward earnings, with the shares above the $235.67 consensus target and about 162.7x fiscal 2028 estimated earnings, the price embeds sustained high-growth outcomes; a slowdown in net new ARR or in net retention would leave little valuation support.

Growth and retention: annual revenue growth has decelerated each year as the base has scaled, and the company notes that dollar-based net retention can fall when customers renew with shorter terms, fewer modules or smaller contract values -- a dynamic the incident's commitment packages can worsen.

GAAP profitability and stock-based compensation: GAAP results remain near breakeven (fiscal 2026 diluted EPS -$0.65; second-quarter $0.01), and the wide gap to non-GAAP income is driven largely by stock-based compensation, so a shareholder relies on free cash flow and must weigh ongoing dilution.

Single-platform concentration: a defect, outage or security failure in the one Falcon platform -- as the July 19 Incident showed -- can affect the entire customer base at once and damage the brand on which new-customer acquisition depends.
risks.systemic: CrowdStrike's results move with the broader technology and macro cycle. Demand for security software is resilient but not immune to enterprise budget tightening in a downturn, which can lengthen sales cycles and slow net new ARR. The equity is a high-multiple, long-duration asset, so it is unusually sensitive to interest rates and to the market's appetite for growth software: a rise in rates or a rotation away from high-multiple names can compress the sales multiple independent of company performance. The company also flags general market, political, economic and business conditions -- including macroeconomic deterioration, inflation, geopolitical conflict and volatility in the financial sector -- as forces that could affect results. As a widely deployed security vendor, CrowdStrike is itself a standing target of cyberattacks, and a compromise of its own systems would harm the reputation on which its franchise depends. These systemic forces bear most on the multiple, which is where the equity's risk is concentrated.

body: We rate CrowdStrike HOLD with a $220-$305 target range that brackets a Base case near $255. The second-quarter fiscal 2027 results were excellent -- revenue up 26% to $1.47 billion, ARR up 25% to $5.84 billion, net new ARR of $333 million, and free cash flow of $377.4 million -- and the moat is wide. But at 49.6x sales and about 208x forward earnings, with the stock above the $235.67 consensus target, the price already reflects that quality, and our probability-weighted fair value sits about 2% below the current $261.28.

The risk/reward is unattractive rather than outright negative: a bear-case de-rating to $185 is a 29% drawdown, while the expected value is roughly flat with today's price. The equity's risk lives in the multiple, not the business -- the July 19, 2024 Incident and a deceleration in annual revenue growth since fiscal 2023 show how expectations can reset even as ARR and free cash flow compound.

We would own CrowdStrike at a lower entry, toward the low end of our range, where the free-cash-flow yield and ARR growth would better compensate for the execution and multiple risk. At $261.28 we wait. The metrics to watch are net new ARR and Falcon Flex momentum, dollar-based net retention, and whether the company converts its non-GAAP profitability into GAAP earnings while beginning to offset stock-based-compensation dilution.
